stories.label: Myanmar junta chief elected as president
stories.summary: Min Aung Hlaing — the general who seized power in a 2021 coup, crushed protests that killed thousands, and is accused of war crimes — just had a parliament he controls 'elect' him president with 429 of 584 votes. The Irrawaddy calls him 'accused war criminal'; Bloomberg calls it an 'election.' Sentiment divergence is 0.71 — the widest in this feed — because the framing gap between Myanmar's critical press and international wire services is the story itself. Lead with the vote count and the word 'elected' in quotes. Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained. 55 million people now live under a coup leader with a constitutional title. The reader should see how military juntas launder power through institutional capture.

stories.label: Cuba pardons 2,010 prisoners amid US pressure
stories.summary: Cuba is releasing 2,010 prisoners — the second mass amnesty this year — framed as a 'Holy Week humanitarian gesture' but timed precisely with ongoing US-Cuba negotiations. The sovereignty framing is the key: Granma calls it a 'sovereign act,' not a concession. SCMP and ThePrint diverge from US outlets on whether this is compliance or defiance (sentimentDivergence 0.38). Lead with the 2,010 number and the Vatican angle — Pope Francis reportedly urged the releases. The reader should see the pattern: small states under US pressure perform concessions they can frame as autonomy. The 'who blinks first' dynamic between Havana and Washington is the structural story.

stories.label: Donald Trump announces next two Iran targets
stories.summary: Five weeks into the war, Trump posted on Truth Social that the US 'hasn't even started destroying what's left in Iran' and named two specific targets — both civilian infrastructure near Karaj and Tehran. This crosses a threshold: explicitly telegraphing strikes on civilian targets on social media. Middle East Eye frames this as escalation; Newsweek's sentiment is positive (0.16). The sentimentDivergence (0.41) reveals how normalized wartime rhetoric has become in some US outlets. Lead with the Truth Social post and the civilian nature of the targets. The reader tracking the Iran war should see this as a shift from military to punitive infrastructure destruction — the Iraq playbook.

stories.label: What South Africa's G7 disinvitation could mean
stories.summary: France withdrew South Africa's G7 invitation — one that Macron personally extended during last year's G20. The timing matters: this follows South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the ICJ and its BRICS chairmanship. Lead with the personal invitation/disinvitation contrast — Macron invited Ramaphosa face-to-face, then his government reversed it. The reader should see this as the G7 disciplining a Global South nation for challenging the Western order. Premium Times (Nigeria) frames this as African agency being punished; the Western framing will be 'diplomatic recalibration.' The ICJ case and BRICS alignment are the unspoken reasons.

stories.label: El-Rufai arrives court for bail hearing
stories.summary: Former Kaduna governor Nasir El-Rufai — once one of Nigeria's most powerful politicians — is in court facing corruption charges from the Independent Corrupt Practices Commission. Three Nigerian sources cover it (Punch, Sahara Reporters, Vanguard) with contrasting tones: Punch is neutral-procedural, Sahara Reporters frames it as overdue accountability. Lead with the power reversal: a governor who wielded enormous authority over Kaduna State now arriving in court under the public gaze. The reader tracking accountability in Africa should see this as a test of whether Nigeria's anti-corruption institutions can actually convict the powerful, not just charge them.

stories.label: Kuwait refinery on fire after another Iranian drone attack
stories.summary: Iranian drones struck Kuwait's Mina al-Ahmadi refinery — a different facility from the desalination plant hit earlier — triggering fires at one of the Gulf's key oil processing sites. The word 'another' in the headline tells the story: Iran is systematically expanding its target set across Gulf oil infrastructure. Lead with the facility name and the pattern — this is the second type of Kuwaiti infrastructure hit, showing Iran is escalating from water to oil. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation confirmed no injuries but operations are under threat. The reader tracking Gulf energy should see the economic consequence: every refinery strike reduces the Gulf's ability to process crude even if extraction continues.

stories.label: Q&A: Kerala taps microbe for health, farming gains
stories.summary: Kerala became the first Indian state to designate a 'state microbe' and is building a microbiome research hub to develop sustainable solutions for health and agriculture. Lead with the novelty: a subnational government treating its microbial ecosystem as a strategic asset, the way states designate official birds or flowers but with actual scientific infrastructure behind it. The reader who thinks about food systems and biotech should see the connection to the fertilizer crisis — microbiome-based farming reduces dependence on synthetic inputs whose supply chains the Hormuz blockade is disrupting. This is Global South science governance innovation, not just academic research.

stories.label: Deep learning-based high-information-content graph representation of early stage bacterial biofilms
stories.summary: Researchers built a deep learning system that maps the 3D architecture of bacterial biofilms during their earliest, most vulnerable formation stage — the moment when antibiotics could actually work. Biofilms are how bacteria become unkillable: they build communal structures that shrug off drugs. Lead with the timing angle: catching biofilms early is the difference between a treatable infection and a chronic one. The graph-based representation captures spatial relationships between individual bacteria, revealing the organizational logic of resistance. The reader who builds software should appreciate the approach: treating a biological colony as a graph problem, where nodes are bacteria and edges are their spatial relationships.

stories.label: High-Resolution Wind Tunnel Dataset of Gas Sensor Responses to Vapor Plumes in Scale Model Landscapes
stories.summary: Researchers released the first high-resolution dataset of how gas sensors on mobile robots and UAVs respond to pollutant plumes in realistic terrain — wind tunnel experiments with scale-model landscapes that simulate real-world pollution tracking. Lead with the application: autonomous robots that can find pollution sources without human guidance. The dataset bridges the gap between lab sensor performance and field deployment. The reader who works with hardware should see the engineering problem: gas sensors on drones behave differently in turbulent air over hills than in a flat lab, and until now there was no data to train algorithms on realistic conditions.

stories.label: Explained: Why Iran hit Amazon's data centres in Bahrain and what it signals for the future of warfare
stories.summary: On March 1, Iranian Shahed drones struck two AWS data centers in the UAE and a third in Bahrain — the first time any country has deliberately targeted civilian cloud computing infrastructure in a military conflict. This Hindustan Times analysis explains the targeting logic: cloud infrastructure is dual-use (it runs both military C2 and civilian services), making it a legal gray zone under international humanitarian law. Lead with the historic first and the dual-use dilemma. A third of the region's cloud capacity went offline, affecting everything from banking to hospital records. The reader who builds on AWS should see the systemic risk: their infrastructure is now a military target because the same data centers serve both Pentagon contracts and consumer apps.

stories.label: Hegseth ousts Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George
stories.summary: Defense Secretary Hegseth forced out the Army's top general during an active war — the first wartime sacking of an Army chief in modern US history. The angle: Trump is purging military leadership for ideological loyalty while US troops are deployed in Iran. Five sources across 5 countries (US, SG, IN, TR, EG) diverge sharply on framing — Al-Ahram calls it 'immediate retirement' while TRT emphasizes the loyalty test. Lead with the wartime context: you don't fire your top general mid-campaign unless the war is going badly or the general is resisting orders. The reader tracking civil-military relations should see the pattern: Hegseth's insider trading allegation (covered yesterday) plus this firing signals a Pentagon in crisis.

stories.label: Trump says Pam Bondi out as attorney general
stories.summary: Trump fired his own attorney general — the nation's top law enforcement officer — over the Epstein files and her failure to prosecute his political enemies aggressively enough. The angle: even ultra-loyalists get discarded when they don't deliver. Bondi had delayed releasing Epstein documents that could implicate Trump allies, and her firing came hours after mounting pressure. Lead with the Epstein connection — the reader should see that the AG was fired not for incompetence but for insufficient complicity. Sentiment divergence 0.44 across US/IN/QA/TR sources suggests radically different framings of the same event.

stories.label: Can Starmer's 40-nation coalition open the Strait of Hormuz?
stories.summary: The UK-led coalition has grown from 35 to 40 nations — but without the US. The angle: a European power is building a multilateral framework to reopen the world's most critical oil chokepoint while the US pursues unilateral military escalation. Bloomberg and FT report the coalition includes France, India, and Japan but faces the core dilemma: Iran has no incentive to negotiate with a coalition that has no military leverage. Lead with the 40-nation number and the US absence — the reader tracking Hormuz should see this as either the post-American world order taking shape or an exercise in diplomatic theater.

stories.label: Pakistan Plays Peacemaker While Bombing and Blockading Afghan Civilians
stories.summary: Pakistan is hosting Saudi-Turkey-Egypt foreign ministers to mediate the Iran war — while simultaneously bombing Afghan civilians on its own western border and blockading humanitarian access. The angle: the hypocrisy is structural, not incidental. A state positioning itself as regional peacemaker is conducting its own war against the most vulnerable people in its territory. Lead with the juxtaposition: Islamabad's diplomatic conference rooms vs the bombed villages on the Afghan border. The reader tracking Pakistan should see how the Iran mediation role provides diplomatic cover for the quieter war at home.

stories.label: Israel Is Conducting a Campaign to Ethnically Cleanse Southern Lebanon of Shia Residents
stories.summary: Drop Site reports from the ground: Israeli forces are systematically clearing Shia villages in southern Lebanon while the Lebanese army stands aside. The angle: this is ethnic cleansing with a sectarian logic — Shia communities are being emptied to create a buffer zone that serves Israeli security at the cost of Lebanese sovereignty. Lead with the abandonment by their own army — residents of border villages expected protection from the LAF and got none. The reader tracking the Lebanon invasion should see how the Litani push (covered earlier) is evolving into permanent demographic engineering.

stories.label: Trump Revamps Steel, Aluminum, Copper Tariffs But Keeps 50% Rate
stories.summary: Trump is 'simplifying' metals tariffs while keeping the 50% rate — a wartime protectionist move that hits every country that exports steel, aluminum, or copper to the US. The angle: the tariff wall is hardening during a global supply shock. With Hormuz disrupting shipping and Iran war driving commodity volatility, a 50% tariff on industrial metals compounds the cost crisis for manufacturers worldwide. Lead with the 50% rate staying put despite industry lobbying — the simplification is cosmetic, the protectionism is structural. Reuters and Bloomberg diverge on framing (sentiment spread 0.18).

stories.label: SpaceX tries to convince FCC that Amazon put satellites into wrong altitude
stories.summary: SpaceX claims Amazon's Project Kuiper satellites were launched at altitudes that create collision risk with Starlink — while SpaceX itself recently had two satellite failures creating new debris. The angle: two billionaire-owned companies are arguing over orbital safety at the FCC while both contribute to the growing space debris problem. Lead with the hypocrisy: SpaceX filed the complaint after its own failures, and Amazon's altitude choices may be a deliberate strategy to avoid Starlink's orbital shells. The reader who follows space infrastructure should see the deeper issue: low Earth orbit is becoming a contested commons with no effective governance.

stories.label: A broadband Terahertz metamaterial absorber enabled by a water-assisted square-pyramid architecture with optical transmittance
stories.summary: Researchers built a metamaterial that absorbs terahertz radiation across a wide bandwidth while remaining optically transparent — cracking a trade-off that has limited THz technology for decades. The angle: terahertz is the 'last frontier' of the electromagnetic spectrum, sitting between microwave and infrared, and this absorber enables practical applications from 6G wireless to security screening to cancer detection. Lead with the dual property (absorbs THz + see-through) and the water-assisted fabrication that makes it scalable. The reader who builds things will appreciate the elegance: using water's dielectric properties as part of the absorber architecture itself.

stories.label: Soil health improvement and climate change mitigation in soybean agroecosystems
stories.summary: Biochar and cover crops can maintain soybean yields while cutting N2O emissions and building soil carbon — reducing dependency on synthetic fertilizers. The angle: with the Hormuz blockade disrupting global fertilizer supply chains (urea and phosphate prices spiking), research showing how to grow food with less synthetic input becomes immediately consequential. Lead with the fertilizer-independence angle: this isn't abstract soil science, it's a food security tool during a supply chain crisis. The reader tracking war ripple effects through food systems should see the connection between Hormuz, fertilizer prices, and the urgent need for alternative soil management.

stories.label: Perplexity's "Incognito Mode" is a "sham," lawsuit says
stories.summary: Perplexity's AI search engine shared complete chat sessions — including those in 'Incognito Mode' — with Google and Meta without user knowledge or consent. The angle: an AI company that markets privacy as a feature is doing the opposite, sharing the most intimate queries (people ask AI things they wouldn't type into Google) with the two largest ad platforms. Lead with the betrayal of trust: Incognito Mode is supposed to mean private, and Perplexity used it as a marketing tool while piping data to advertisers. The reader who uses AI search daily should see the structural lesson: 'privacy mode' in a VC-funded AI company is a UI element, not a guarantee.

stories.label: Cursor 3
stories.summary: Cursor 3 launches as the AI coding editor war intensifies — 188 HN points and 154 comments signal strong developer engagement. The angle: AI-assisted coding tools are now shipping fast enough that major version releases happen quarterly, and developers are reorganizing their workflows around them. Lead with what's new in Cursor 3 that makes developers excited (the HN discussion has 154 comments — unusually high signal for a product launch). The reader who codes daily should see this as the next step in the AI coding agent evolution that includes Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Windsurf — the competitive dynamics matter as much as the features.

stories.label: Austria rejects US request to use airspace for Iran operations
stories.summary: Austria invoked its constitutional neutrality to refuse 'several' US requests for overflight rights for Iran operations. The angle: a neutral European country is drawing a legal line against the US war machine — the same neutrality doctrine that kept Austria out of NATO. Lead with the constitutional mechanism and the word 'several' (repeated requests imply escalating pressure). The reader tracking the war's diplomatic fallout should see this as a fracture in the Western consensus: not every US ally is compliant. TRT World and MEE diverge on framing — compare the sovereignty vs alliance angles.

stories.label: The War You're Not Allowed to See: How the UAE Rewrites the Story of Iranian Strikes
stories.summary: Bellingcat used open-source satellite imagery and social media to identify multiple incidents where UAE authorities downplayed damage, mischaracterised interceptions, or failed to acknowledge successful Iranian drone strikes. The angle: a Gulf state is running an information war alongside the military war — and OSINT can prove it. Lead with the gap between official UAE statements and observable reality. The reader tracking the war should see how information control shapes perception of who is 'winning.' This is the kind of accountability journalism only OSINT can deliver when states control the narrative.

stories.label: U.S.-Israeli strikes target Iran's healthcare system
stories.summary: Drop Site reports that US-Israeli strikes are hitting Iran's healthcare infrastructure — hospitals, clinics, supply chains. The angle: targeting healthcare is a potential war crime under international humanitarian law, and it compounds the suffering of 88 million Iranian civilians already under wartime stress. Lead with the healthcare infrastructure being destroyed — the reader who saw the BBC testimony of desperate Iranians should now see the structural mechanism causing that desperation. This is accountability reporting: name the actors, name the targets, name the law.

stories.label: Israeli leaders are condemning settler attacks. It's a smokescreen
stories.summary: +972 argues that the recent wave of denunciations of settler violence from Israeli ministers, army chiefs, and right-wing pundits is a deliberate smokescreen to obscure that settler violence IS state policy. The angle: when the powerful condemn their own tools, ask what they're distracting from. Lead with the paradox — the same government that arms and protects settlers is now 'condemning' them. The reader should see the structural pattern: performative condemnation as cover for continued dispossession. This is a ground-level analysis from journalists living under the system they're reporting on.

stories.label: Nine states record over 10,000 IDPs in two months — NHRC
stories.summary: Nigeria's National Human Rights Commission reports 10,884 people displaced across 9 states in just January-February 2026, calling it a 'persistent and growing protection crisis.' The angle: internal displacement in Nigeria is accelerating but invisible — no international headlines, no emergency summits. Lead with the number and the speed (10,000+ in 60 days). Benue and Borno states are the worst hit. The reader should see the pattern: when the world's attention is consumed by Iran and Hormuz, Africa's displacement crises deepen in silence.

stories.label: Tesla Q1 deliveries miss Wall Street expectations despite bounce-back hopes
stories.summary: Tesla delivered 358,023 vehicles in Q1 — down 14.4% from Q4 and below analyst expectations — as the expiry of US EV tax credits hit demand. Shares slid on the news. The angle: the world's most politically connected CEO (DOGE, White House access) can't translate political power into sales. Lead with the 14.4% quarter-over-quarter decline and the tax credit expiry. Europe and China are both weakening for Tesla. The reader tracking Musk's dual role in government and business should see the accountability dimension: market consequences catch up even when political protection doesn't.

stories.label: Walmart Recession Signal at highest since 2008 financial crisis
stories.summary: The Walmart Recession Signal (WRS) — which tracks the gap between Walmart's stock performance and the broader market as a proxy for consumer downtrading — has surged to levels last seen during the 2008 financial crisis. The angle: when consumers flee to Walmart, it means middle-class purchasing power is collapsing. Lead with the 2008 comparison and explain the mechanism: Walmart outperforming the market is a sign of distress, not health. The reader tracking Hormuz-driven inflation and the war economy should see this as the domestic consumer signal confirming what oil prices already suggest.

stories.label: Elliptic flags $285 million Drift exploit as likely North Korea-linked operation
stories.summary: Blockchain forensics firm Elliptic has attributed the $285M Drift Protocol exploit — the largest DeFi hack of 2026 — to North Korean state hackers, based on laundering patterns matching Lazarus Group tactics. This advances the existing Drift story with the critical 'who': a sanctioned state using Solana's fragmented account model to fund weapons programs. Lead with the NK attribution and the laundering methodology — cross-chain mixing that exploits Solana's architecture. The reader who tracks both crypto and geopolitics should see the convergence: DeFi vulnerabilities are now a national security issue.

stories.label: Heterostructure-engineered diamond-graphene composites for high-performance electromagnetic wave absorption
stories.summary: Researchers created a diamond-graphene heterostructure that simultaneously delivers strong electromagnetic wave attenuation and survives extreme environments — cracking a long-standing trade-off in stealth/radar-absorbing materials. The angle: this is materials science with immediate defense and aerospace applications. Current stealth coatings degrade under heat and stress; this composite doesn't. Lead with the dual breakthrough (absorbs radar + survives harsh conditions) and the defense implication. The reader who builds things will appreciate the engineering elegance of solving a decades-old materials trade-off.

stories.label: Google announces Gemma 4 open AI models, switches to Apache 2.0 license
stories.summary: Google released Gemma 4, its open-weight AI model family, and switched from a restrictive custom license to Apache 2.0 — the gold standard for open source. The angle: this is Google conceding that open-source AI needs to be actually open to compete. Lead with the license change (Apache 2.0 means anyone can use, modify, and commercialize) and the competitive pressure from Meta's Llama and Alibaba's Qwen. HN discussion (183 points, 30 comments) signals developer enthusiasm. The reader who builds with AI should see the strategic shift: Google is betting that ecosystem adoption matters more than control.

stories.label: A Secure Chat App's Encryption Is So Bad It Is 'Meaningless'
stories.summary: TeleGuard, a 'secure' messaging app with over a million downloads, uploads users' private keys to the company's server — making its end-to-end encryption completely meaningless. The angle: people in high-risk environments (journalists, activists, dissidents) may be trusting their safety to an app that is architecturally incapable of protecting them. Lead with the private key upload — any developer will immediately understand the severity. The reader who uses encrypted messaging daily should see the structural lesson: marketing 'security' is trivial, verifying it requires reading the code.

stories.label: Journalist Sues FAA Over Drone No Fly Zone Designed to Prevent Filming ICE
stories.summary: A Minnesota journalist is suing the FAA over a 3,000-foot no-fly zone around DHS/ICE assets, arguing it was designed specifically to prevent drone journalism of immigration enforcement. The angle: the government is using airspace regulation as a censorship tool — a First Amendment challenge to the surveillance state's attempt to operate without witnesses. Lead with the 3,000-foot restriction and its targeted purpose. The reader who follows both press freedom and surveillance tech should see the pattern: when the state doesn't want to be watched, it doesn't ban cameras — it bans the sky.

stories.label: Qwen3.6-Plus: Towards Real World Agents
stories.summary: Alibaba's Qwen team released Qwen 3.6-Plus, positioning it as an AI model specifically designed for real-world agent tasks — autonomous tool use, multi-step reasoning, and environment interaction. The angle: China's open-weight AI models are now competing directly with Google's Gemma 4 (released the same day) on the frontier of AI agents. Lead with the timing: two major open AI model releases on the same day, from the US and China. HN discussion (185 points, 66 comments) shows developer community taking Chinese models seriously. The reader building with AI should see the geopolitical dimension: the AI agent race is now a two-front competition.

stories.label: Iran fires missiles at Israel and Gulf neighbors as Trump talks of winding down Mideast war
stories.summary: Iran launched another wave of missiles at Israel and Gulf Arab states on Day 28 of the war — even as Trump claimed the threat was 'nearly eliminated.' The angle: the gap between Washington's victory narrative and Tehran's demonstrated strike capability. Lead with the continued strikes on Gulf neighbors, not just Israel — the reader tracking Hormuz should see that the war zone is expanding, not contracting. This undercuts the UK Hormuz conference happening the same day.

stories.label: 'In safe hands': Iran reassures 'Indian friends' on passage through Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: Iran is offering bilateral Hormuz passage agreements to European, Asian, and Arab countries — bypassing the US-led coalition framework entirely. The angle: Tehran is splitting the Western bloc by offering a diplomatic alternative to military escort. India is the first named partner. Lead with the geopolitical judo: while the UK convenes 30+ nations for a coalition, Iran is offering individual deals that make a coalition unnecessary for any country willing to negotiate directly. The reader tracking Hormuz should see the fracture lines forming.

stories.label: SC halts anti-terrorism court from framing charges against journalist Matiullah Jan
stories.summary: Pakistan's Supreme Court blocked an anti-terrorism court from framing charges against veteran journalist Matiullah Jan, directing the Islamabad High Court to expedite its challenge to the terrorism charges. The angle: a journalist is being prosecuted under anti-terror laws — the same legal architecture meant for armed militants is being turned on press critics. Lead with the legal mechanism: terrorism charges against a journalist, and a Supreme Court that intervened. The reader should see the press freedom dimension in a country already under dual pressure from the Iran war's economic ripple effects.

stories.label: Italy fines Revolut over misleading fees and terms details
stories.summary: Italy's competition watchdog fined Revolut €11.5mn for advertising '0% commission' trading while burying real costs in fine print. The angle: Europe's most valuable fintech startup (valued at $45bn) is being held accountable by a regulator in a market where it's aggressively expanding. Lead with the '0% commission' lie — the reader who uses fintech daily will recognize the pattern. The structural point: EU regulators are testing whether fintech companies face the same consumer protection standards as traditional banks.

stories.label: RWA news: France's tokenized stock exchange Lise poised for first onchain IPO in Europe
stories.summary: France's Lightning Stock Exchange (Lise) is preparing Europe's first fully onchain IPO — listing aerospace firm ST Group on a blockchain-native exchange operating within EU regulatory frameworks. The angle: this isn't crypto-native speculation, it's a regulated stock market built on blockchain rails. Lead with the precedent: if it works, smaller European firms get a cheaper, faster path to public markets without the overhead of traditional exchanges. The reader tracking tokenization (after Brazil's B3 bitcoin derivatives) should see the pattern: traditional finance is absorbing blockchain infrastructure, not the other way around.

stories.label: Fuel prices are soaring. Plastic could be next.
stories.summary: The Hormuz bottleneck is now hitting petrochemical feedstock for plastics — which account for 5% of global CO2 emissions and touch everything from medical devices to food packaging. The angle: this is the next cascade after fuel. India already invoked emergency powers to restructure its chemical supply chain (covered yesterday). Lead with the universality: plastic is in everything, and its precursors flow through the same choke point as oil. The reader tracking Hormuz ripple effects should see the supply chain extending from fuel → petrochemicals → plastics → consumer goods.

stories.label: CDC stops testing for rabies, pox viruses
stories.summary: The CDC has halted testing for rabies and pox viruses — diseases with near-100% fatality rates if untreated. The angle: this isn't budget trimming, it's eliminating the diagnostic capacity for lethal pathogens. Rabies kills ~60,000 people globally per year; the US is the reference lab for much of the Western Hemisphere. Lead with the fatality rate and the diagnostic monopoly: if the CDC stops testing, who does? The reader should see this as infrastructure decay in real time — the same pattern as the DOGE-era NIH grant cuts.

stories.label: Engineering multiple levels of specificity in an RNA viral vector - Nature Communications
stories.summary: Researchers engineered an RNA-based viral vector (derived from rabies virus) that can be programmed to target only specific cell types — stacking multiple layers of specificity so the therapeutic payload activates only in diseased cells. The angle: this is programmable medicine at the delivery level. Current gene therapies are blunt instruments; this adds an 'if-then' logic layer to the vehicle itself. Lead with the precision: a virus that infects only the cells you want, and only activates its cargo when it confirms it's in the right place. The reader who builds software will recognize the pattern — conditional execution, but in biology.

stories.label: I have been bitten by more than 200 snakes - on purpose
stories.summary: Tim Friede has intentionally subjected himself to 200+ venomous snake bites to develop self-immunization against snakebite — a neglected tropical disease that kills 138,000 and disables 400,000 people per year, mostly in rural Africa and South Asia. The angle: the world's most neglected medical crisis (WHO's own label) has so little funding that a single self-experimenter has become a significant research subject. Lead with the 5 million bites per year and the funding gap — then the man who made himself the experiment. The reader should see the structural failure: Big Pharma won't invest because the victims are poor.

stories.label: IBM Announces Strategic Collaboration with Arm
stories.summary: IBM and Arm announced a strategic collaboration to bring Arm-based processors into enterprise computing — a domain that has been x86 territory for decades. The angle: this is the server architecture shift reaching its endgame. Apple moved to Arm in 2020; cloud providers followed with Graviton and Ampere; now IBM is bringing its enterprise middleware stack (WebSphere, Db2, the mainframe ecosystem) to Arm. Lead with what changes: the last bastion of x86 dominance — mission-critical enterprise workloads — is being contested. HN discussion (100+ points, 54 comments) signals the developer community sees this as significant.

stories.label: Email obfuscation: What works in 2026?
stories.summary: A systematic study of which email obfuscation techniques actually prevent harvesting by bots in 2026 — testing CSS tricks, JavaScript encoding, SVG rendering, and more against modern scrapers and LLM-powered crawlers. The angle: the arms race between spam harvesters and obfuscation has a new player — AI crawlers that can 'read' obfuscated emails the way humans do. Lead with what's changed: techniques that worked in 2020 are broken because LLM-powered bots understand context. HN discussion (172 points, 50 comments) shows developers are actively rethinking a problem they thought was solved.

stories.label: Four astronauts depart for the Moon with a fiery send-off from Cape Canaveral
stories.summary: Artemis II launched — three Americans and one Canadian aboard the most powerful rocket ever ridden by humans, on the first crewed lunar mission in 54 years. Victor Glover becomes the first Black astronaut to fly to the Moon. Lead with the human milestone: the last time anyone did this, Nixon was president. But also note the context the reader cares about: this mission launches while NASA faces budget cuts, the Space Force plans to follow, and SpaceX just filed to go public. The Moon race is resuming as a multi-actor contest, not an Apollo reprise.

stories.label: Australia to offer businesses $693 million in cheap loans to ease fuel cost pressure
stories.summary: Australia imports 80%+ of its fuel and the Iran war has triggered panic buying despite government assurances. Albanese announces $693M in cheap loans for businesses plus a GST deal knocking 32 cents off petrol. Lead with the dependency: a wealthy G20 nation is scrambling because it outsourced its energy security. The reader tracking Hormuz ripple effects should see: Australia is the first Western country to deploy fiscal stimulus specifically to manage the Iran war's fuel shock. Previous cycles covered Pakistan and India's fuel crises — this is the rich-country version.

stories.label: 'They already shoot us for no reason. Now they have a death penalty'
stories.summary: Israel's parliament passed a law mandating the death penalty exclusively for Palestinian prisoners convicted of lethal attacks labeled 'terrorism' — with no possibility of pardon or commutation. Amnesty International calls it 'one of the world's most extreme death penalty laws.' Lead with the exclusivity: only Palestinians face capital punishment under this law. A tribunal for Oct. 7 convictions is next. The reader tracking Palestine should see: the legal architecture of occupation is hardening — this isn't martial law improvisation, it's statutory permanence. Two independent outlets (+972 ground reporting, Mada Masr legal analysis) confirm the details.

stories.label: Map: 7.4-Magnitude Earthquake Strikes in Indonesia
stories.summary: A 7.4-magnitude quake struck the Molucca Sea, triggering tsunami warnings for Indonesia, the Philippines, and Malaysia. The epicenter near Ternate puts one of Indonesia's most volcanically active regions on alert. Lead with the scale and the cascading risk — tsunami + aftershocks in a region of 270 million people. The structural why: Indonesia sits on the Ring of Fire, and its early warning systems were rebuilt after the 2004 disaster but remain uneven across the eastern archipelago.

stories.label: Drones hit oil refinery in Russia's Ufa, large-scale fire breaks out
stories.summary: Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Ufa — over 1,200km from the frontline — setting off a large-scale fire. Air defense intercepted 147 drones overnight but couldn't stop the refinery hit. Lead with the range: Ufa is deep in Bashkortostan, not a border region. This shows Ukraine's deep-strike drone capability now reaches Russia's industrial heartland. The reader should see the energy angle: Russia's refining capacity is being systematically degraded while it extends its own gasoline export ban.

stories.label: Trump 'threatened to stop supplying weapons for Ukraine'
stories.summary: Trump threatened to cut Ukraine's weapons supply unless European nations join a coalition to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Lead with the linkage: two separate wars are now being traded against each other as bargaining chips. Ukraine's survival is being used as leverage for Hormuz. The reader should see the power dynamic: the US is the only country supplying Ukraine at scale, and Trump is weaponizing that dependency to recruit a reluctant Europe into the Iran conflict.

stories.label: India ends import tax on petrochemicals to help local industry
stories.summary: India invoked emergency powers to abolish import duties on petrochemicals after diverting domestic chemicals to cooking gas production due to Iran war shortages. This affects plastics, pharmaceuticals, and textiles for 1.4 billion people. Lead with the emergency powers: a G20 nation is restructuring its chemical supply chain mid-crisis because the Iran war redirected feedstock. The reader tracking Hormuz ripple effects should see the cascade: war → fuel shortage → chemical diversion → import duty removal → dependency on foreign petrochemicals.

stories.label: Save 'Every Drop of Fuel' South Korea Urges, as Iran Crisis Hits
stories.summary: South Korea's president told the National Assembly to 'save every drop of fuel' as the Iran war squeezes the world's 5th-largest oil importer. Korea imports nearly all its energy. Lead with the image: the president of a $1.7T economy is asking citizens to conserve fuel — a wartime austerity signal from a country not at war. The reader should see: this is the East Asian version of Pakistan's rationing and Australia's fuel loans. The Hormuz closure is creating a rolling crisis across every import-dependent economy.

stories.label: Gulf countries considering new oil export routes  --  FT
stories.summary: Gulf states are discussing pipeline expansion to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, including expanding Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. The FT reports this as the first serious infrastructure pivot since the blockade began. Lead with the strategic shift: if producers build around Hormuz, Iran's leverage over global oil flows diminishes permanently. This is the long-term play — not a diplomatic resolution but a physical rerouting of the world's energy arteries.

stories.label: Masdar and TotalEnergies to form $2.2bn joint renewable energy venture
stories.summary: Abu Dhabi's Masdar and France's TotalEnergies are merging their Asian and Central Asian renewable portfolios into a $2.2 billion JV covering Japan, Indonesia, and Azerbaijan. Lead with the timing: two fossil-fuel-adjacent giants are pooling $2.2B in clean energy while the world scrambles for oil because of the Hormuz blockade. The reader should see the hedge: Gulf states aren't just planning pipeline bypasses — they're accelerating the post-oil transition in the same week.

stories.label: Attention bitcoin traders. These indicators matter more than what Trump says about Iran
stories.summary: Ship insurance premiums for Hormuz transits and collapsed tanker traffic are the real indicators — not Trump's statements. Bitcoin at $66,481 is reacting to political noise while the physical blockade data shows the route remains unsafe. Lead with the divergence: markets chase tweets while shipping data tells the real story. The reader who trades crypto and follows oil futures needs the signal-vs-noise framing: insurance premiums and AIS vessel tracking are the leading indicators, not presidential rhetoric.

stories.label: Ban on gasoline exports from Russia extended to producers of petroleum products
stories.summary: Russia extended its gasoline export ban through July 2026 and widened it to include direct producers — not just traders. Lead with what changed: the ban now covers producers themselves, meaning Russia's refiners can't sell a drop abroad. Read alongside the Ufa refinery strike: Ukraine is destroying Russia's refining capacity while Russia simultaneously hoards what remains for domestic consumption. The war is creating two simultaneous fuel crises — one external (Hormuz), one internal (Russian refining).

stories.label: Steam on Linux Use Skyrocketed Above 5% in March
stories.summary: Steam's Linux user share crossed 5% for the first time in March — up from under 1% five years ago. 259 HN points. Lead with the trajectory: Linux gaming went from joke to 1-in-20 Steam users, driven by the Steam Deck and Proton compatibility layer. The reader is a hacker who cares about open platforms — this is validation that the desktop Linux ecosystem is reaching critical mass in the one domain (gaming) that always held it back.

stories.label: Subscription bombing and how to mitigate it
stories.summary: Your signup form is a weapon: attackers use subscription bombing to flood a target's inbox with thousands of confirmation emails from legitimate services, burying real messages. 114 HN points, 79 comments. Lead with the mechanism: no exploit is needed — the attacker just submits the victim's email to every newsletter signup they can find. The reader who builds web apps should see the defense gap: most signup forms lack rate limiting or confirmation delays that would stop this.

stories.label: EXCLUSIVE: The mystery of Minister Sisisi Tolashe's missing SUVs
stories.summary: South Africa's Social Development Minister told Parliament that two luxury SUVs from Chinese officials were donations to the ANC Women's League. Daily Maverick's investigation suggests the BAIC vehicles were given to Tolashe's two children for personal use. Lead with the lie to Parliament: a cabinet minister misrepresented gifts from a foreign government. The China influence angle matters — BAIC is a state-linked automaker. The reader should see the accountability gap: the minister lied on record and there's no mechanism forcing consequences.

stories.label: Croatia's Football Team Signed Deal With Gambling Sponsor Whose Rep Used Fake Name
stories.summary: A European academic used a false name to represent an opaque Asian-facing bookmaker sponsoring Croatia's national football team ahead of the 2026 World Cup. Bellingcat + Josimar joint investigation. Lead with the deception: a fake identity brokering a deal between a national team and an unregulated gambling company. The reader should see the pattern — opaque money from offshore gambling flows into football via intermediaries who don't even use real names. World Cup sponsorship is the laundering mechanism.

stories.label: Trump administration prepares 100% tariffs on some imported drugs
stories.summary: The Trump administration has prepared a 100% tariff on imports of patented medications and their active ingredients — potentially doubling the cost of brand-name drugs overnight. Could be announced Thursday. Lead with the 100% number: this isn't a nudge, it's a wall. Section 232 national security authority is the mechanism — the same tool used for steel tariffs, now applied to pharmaceuticals. The reader should see the cascade: drug companies will pass costs to insurers, insurers to patients. Countries that manufacture generics (India, Ireland) face export devastation.

stories.label: SpaceX files to go public
stories.summary: SpaceX has filed for an IPO — opening the most valuable private company in the world to public markets. 242 HN points, 309 comments. Lead with the valuation gap: SpaceX was last valued at ~$350B privately. A public listing forces real price discovery on a company that launches national security payloads, dominates commercial space, and is run by a government official (DOGE). The reader in tech should see the conflict: Musk sets government space policy while his company is the primary beneficiary of government space contracts.

stories.label: Sources: Despite EGX listings, govt unlikely launch offerings in current economic conditions
stories.summary: Egypt listed 10 state-owned companies on the stock exchange to 'great praise from international institutions' — but sources say the government has no intention of actually selling shares in current conditions. Lead with the theater: the listing is the announcement, not the action. Egypt's privatization program has been a series of promises to the IMF that never materialize. The reader tracking Egypt should see this alongside yesterday's military tribunal story — the same government that criminalizes merchants for raising prices is pretending to liberalize its economy.

stories.label: Integrated pollution and carbon mitigation delivers major health and economic co-benefits in China
stories.summary: A Nature study quantifies what China gains by cutting pollution and carbon simultaneously: province-level data shows coordinated mitigation delivers health and economic returns that exceed the cost of action. Lead with the finding that contradicts the 'economy vs. environment' framing — the co-benefits are positive, not a tradeoff. The reader should see the policy implication: China's provinces have granular evidence that decarbonization pays for itself through reduced healthcare costs and productivity gains. This is the data other developing countries need.

stories.label: Mohmand's unregulated marble industry raises environmental, safety concerns
stories.summary: Mohmand district's marble industry — a key employer — is destroying waterways with untreated slurry, silting dams, and raising flood risk for surrounding communities. Lead with the tradeoff that isn't: the industry creates jobs while poisoning the water those workers' families drink. Irrigation and water storage are being undermined in a region already vulnerable to climate-driven flooding. The reader should see the pattern across the Global South: extractive industries in ungoverned spaces export profits and leave environmental debt.

stories.label: DRAM pricing is killing the hobbyist SBC market
stories.summary: DRAM prices have spiked so severely that hobbyist single-board computers (Raspberry Pi, etc.) are becoming unaffordable — the components that make a $35 computer possible now cost more than the computer itself. 356 HN points, 288 comments. Lead with the price inversion: memory chips now cost more than the processor on a hobbyist board. The reader who tinkers with hardware should see the structural cause: DRAM is a cartel market (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) and AI datacenter demand is eating the supply that used to keep consumer prices low. The democratization of computing is being reversed by the AI boom.

stories.label: What's real anymore? AI warps truth of Middle East war
stories.summary: AI-generated disinformation is eroding the ability to verify what's real in the Middle East war — a Netanyahu video sparked 'Is this AI?' debates (it was real), while actual AI fakes of Gaza destruction circulate unchallenged. Lead with the epistemological collapse: when people can't tell real footage from fake, both truth and lies lose their power. The reader building AI should see the deeper problem: the doubt itself is the weapon. You don't need to fake a video if you've trained everyone to distrust all video.
